doc.title: John Best interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Wartime choices and Shaw's Navy band
summary: After Miller broke up, Best chose Shaw's Navy band under Sam Donahue and was sent to England.

bands.name: Glenn Miller Army Air Force Band

blocks.x: Oh, that’s true, yeah. Well what happened to you during the war years? What was your experience during World War II?

Mine? Well I survived for one thing. I didn’t want to get drafted. After the Miller band broke up, in September of ‘42, in Passaic, New Jersey, I joined the Bob Crosby band. And that lasted six weeks and that band broke up at that time. In the meantime during that period I got a call from Artie Shaw, that he was recruiting a band of professional musicians for the Navy. And their job would be to play for the troops, the military, as close to the action of the war as they would send us. And he told me who was in the band, he said Davy Tough, Max Kaminsky, Claude Thornhill and Sam Donahue. And it sounded like a good group, which it was, and meantime Miller had said he got a commission to go in the Army, and he got a Captain’s commission and he had also said, “Don’t do anything military until you get in touch with me.” He said, “I am going to get a band in the military, or I am going to resign my commission.” He was over age. Well and then I also had another thing from a band, a Navy band that said they would hold a place for me in Norfolk, Virginia. That was Saxie Dowell. I don’t know whether that name rings a bill — he was a saxophone player with Hal Kemp for years, and he was in charge of this Navy band at Norfolk. And Dean Kincaid, a saxophone player, was in that band, a good friend. Well they came to New York one summer, the summer of ‘42, and they said they would hold a position for me until I made up my mind. So I actually had three ways — I didn’t want to get drafted. There you have no choice. I had the attitude that if I could survive the war and still be able to make a living playing the horn, that’s what I wanted to do. But if you go — I knew people, a good trumpet player that drove a tank — he never played the horn again the rest of his life. So I was fortunate enough to get with that band © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

and stay — Shaw was discharged. They threatened to break the band up then and send us out as replacements. But somebody in Washington said keep the group together, you’ve got an excellent group. So Sam Donahue was the leader. They sent us to England for a year, and that’s where we had battle music with Glenn’s Army band, on the Londonderry Club in London. The Queensbury Club, I said Londonderry, Queensbury.
When you had a battle, each band played like a half hour or something, and the audience decided who they liked the best?

The way it’s set, I have a picture of it, the Miller band there were, they had 21 strings in it, and our band at this stage, we had an excellent band I mean musically — you couldn’t — I still hear tapes of that Army band and musically it was ahead — well he had more choice, for selection. Where did we leave off?
You were talking about the battle between Artie Shaw and Glenn Miller.
Well that was Sam Donahue now.

After Shaw was discharged, after a year in the Pacific, and they threatened to break that band up and send us out as replacements. Now the other band that I had a choice of going with, they wound up on the Franklin Carrier which was blown off the map practically. It survived the bombing but they had eleven hundred casualties or something like that. I don’t know about the band. I know Kincaid survived I know that, and so did the leader.
So that turned out to be a pretty important decision you had made at that point.
You can’t look ahead and see that coming.
Did you get into Europe with the Donahue band?
Before that band. After I mean I got into Europe with the Ray Conniff band you know. And also, South America.
